This revision having been heard and reserved for judgment/order,
coming on for pronouncement this day, this Court passed the following:
 ORDER

The present revision has been filed challenging the order dated 07.03.2024 passed by the learned appellate Court whereby the application filed by the present petitioners under Section 391 of Cr.P.C.
for adducing additional evidence has been rejected.

2. The brief facts leading to the present controversy as advanced by learned senior counsel for the petitioners are that the present petitioners were prosecuted for offencse under Section 7(ii) /16 (1)(a)
(ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 (for short hereinafter referred to as Act of 1954).

The present petitioners have been convicted for the aforesaid offence with sentence of one year R.I.
and fine.
Against the judgment of conviction and sentence dated 16.10.2019 passed by the trial court, the present petitioners have filed appeal before the Sessions Court which is pending.

During pendency of the said appeal the present petitioners filed an application under Section 391 of Cr.P.C.
to summon one Sanjay Arora who is proprietor of "Sugar Dealer" which is a firm from which the questioned commodity is said to be purchased by the petitioners.

3. The substratum of the prosecution case against the present petitioners is that the present petitioners are the Manager and Proprietor of one restaurant establishment namely "Hotel Prestige Princess" and on 17.06.2011 there was a inspection in the said hotel by the concerned authority and during the course of inspection, it was found that some packets of Chinese Noodles were kept in the restaurant and team purchased three packets of noodles on payment of price of the said packets and obtained receipt.

When the said noodles were subjected to examination in the laboratory, then though no harmful or injurious adulterants were found in the packets of noodles but the packets were found to be mis-branded.

4. Learned counsel for the petitioners submits that as per Section 19 of the Act of 1954, it is provided in sub-section (2) that the vendor shall not be deemed to have committed an offence pertaining to sale of any adulterated or mis-branded food articles article of food if he proves that he purchased the article of food from any manufacturer, distributor or dealer, with a written warranty in the prescribed form.

It is further argued that as per proviso to Section 14, the bill, cash memorandum or invoice issued by a vendor of the article shall be deemed to be a warranty given by such manufacturer, distributor or dealer under this section.

Thus, it is argued that the present petitioners had purchased the packets of noodles from "Sugar Dealer"
firm and the deposition of proprietor of that firm is necessary to prove warranty.
It is further argued that in terms of Section 20 (A) of Act 1954 the Court can proceed suo-motu against the manufacturer, distributor or dealer of any article of food.

Thus,

sentences.text: it is contended that even if petitioners had not requested for summoning the proprietor of such firm, even than the trial court as well as appellate court were duty bound to implead the said person as accused.
Thus, it is contended that to prove the innocence of present petitioners, the deposition of Sanjay Arora, proprietor of "Sugar Dealer" is essential.

It is further contended by learned senior counsel that the sole consideration of application under Section 391 of Cr.P.C. at appellate stage should be to meet the ends of justice and mere filing of application at belated stage is not a sufficient ground to reject the application.
The judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Brigadier Sukhjeet Singh (Retired) MVC Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and others 2019 (16) SCC 712 is relied.

sentences.text:
5. Per contra, learned counsel for the State has opposed the revision and has contended that the petitioners have filed the application belatedly and petitioners were given full opportunity to prove their innocence during the course of the trial and now to fill up the lacuna they cannot be allowed to misuse and abuse the provision of Section 391 of Cr.P.C.
6.
Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record.

7. In the present case the contention of petitioners is that they need to prove the bill so as to substantiate the defence in terms of Section 14 of Act of 1954 on the ground that they had purchased the food articles under warranty from the dealer.
They want to proprietor of that "Sugar Dealer" firm to prove that the food articles were in fact purchased under the bill from that vendor.

8. Upon perusal of the documents placed on record with this revision it is evident that the bill/invoice raised by "Sugar Dealer"
was duly brought on record by the present petitioners during the defence evidence and the bill was marked as Ex. D/1 and proved by DW/1.

The petitioners had examined one Rajesh who is Manager in the hotel of the petitioners to prove the bill Ex. D-1.
9.

It is clear from the above facts that the petitioners were prosecuting the trial with diligence and had duly taken care to produce the bill as Ex. D\1 to substantiate their defence in terms of Section 14 and 19 of the Act of 1954.
They chose to examine their own manager to prove the bill and to not choose to examine the proprietor of the firm who issued the bill, to prove the said bill.

10. Sections 233, 243 and 247 of the Cr.P.C. contain clear provision that the accused if he enters upon his defence can apply to the Court to compel the attendance of any witness to substantiate his defence.
It is evident that the petitioners were having this opportunity during the course of trial in terms of Section 243 and 247 of the Cr.P.C. which they do not seem to have availed.
It is not a case where a new document has come on record which was not within the power, possession or knowledge of the petitioners.

The petitioners fully alive to the fact that they are in possession of a bill of the food articles and they need to prove the bill so as to substantiate their defence in terms of Parag Audholia vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 5 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/58243131/
3 Section 14 and 19 of the Act of 1954. The petitioners could have moved an application under Section 243 and 247 of Cr.P.C. to summon the said person Sanjay Arora in their defence to prove the bill Ex.
D/1.

sentences.text: However, that chance was never availed by the petitioners, thus, the request at this stage of appeal to summon Sanjay Arora as witness to prove the bill seems to be an attempt to fill up the lacuna.
11. The trial in the present case continued for as many as 8 years and the petitioners did not avail the opportunity under Section 243 and 247 of Cr.P.C during course of the trial.

The bill has been filed in the year 2019 after conviction and the application under Section 391 of Cr.P.C. for calling Sanjay Arora has been filed only in the year 2024 i.e. after 5 years of filing of appeal,
that too at the stage when the appeal is being posted for final arguments.

12. So far as the reliance on the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Brigadier Sukhjeet Singh (Retired) MVC Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and others 2019 (16) SCC 712 is concerned,
the said case turns on different factual back ground.

entities.text: Brigadier Sukhjeet Singh (Retired) MVC Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and others 2019 (16) SCC 712
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the said case a trust deed was on record but the trial court had refused to relied on the trust deed only because its photocopy was on record and its original was not on record.
During the appellate stage the accused persons had brought on record the certified copy of the trust deed and that was not allowed to be taken on record.

In these circumstances, the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that the certified copy of trust deed can be taken on record by appellate Court by exercising jurisdiction of u/s 391 Cr.P.C. to meet ends of justice.
13. On the other hand, in the present case, the facts as narrated above indicate that the petitioners seek to invoke section 391 of Cr.P.C. to fill up lacuna.

14. Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Zahira Habibullah Sheikh & Anr vs State Of Gujarat & Ors 2004(4) SCC 158 has held that Section 391 of the Code is another salutary provision which clothes the courts with the power to effectively decide an appeal.

entities.text: Zahira Habibullah Sheikh & Anr vs State Of Gujarat & Ors 2004(4) SCC 158
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Though Section 386 envisages the normal and ordinary manner and method of disposal of an appeal, yet it does not and cannot be said to exhaustively enumerate the modes by which alone the court can deal with an appeal.
Section 391 is one such exception to the ordinary rule.
For this purpose it is open to the appellate court to call for further evidence before the appeal is disposed of.

The appellate court can direct the taking up of further evidence in support of the prosecution; a fortiori it is open to the court to direct that the accused persons may also be given a chance of adducing further evidence.
The primary object of Section 391 is the prevention of a guilty man's escape through some careless or ignorant proceedings before a court or vindication of an innocent person wrongfully accused.
Where the court through some carelessness or ignorance has omitted to record the circumstances essential to elucidation of truth, the exercise of powers under Section 391 is desirable.

In the present case, the non- availing of the opportunity during course of trial u/s 243 and 247 Cr.P.C. does not appear out of ignorance or carelessness of the petitioners as they have been shown to be dilligently prosecuting their defence in the trial.

15. In a recent judgment, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Ajitsinh Chehuji Rathod Vs. State of Gujarat and Another 2024 SCC OnLine SC 77 has held as under:-

sentences.text: Thus, we are of the view that if at all, the appellant was desirous of proving that the signatures as appearing on the cheque issued from his account were not genuine,

then he could have procured a certified copy of his specimen signatures from the Bank and a request could have been made to summon the concerned Bank official in defence for giving evidence regarding the genuineness or otherwise of the signature on the cheque.
18.

However, despite having opportunity, the accused appellant did not put any question to the bank official examined in defence for establishing his plea of purported mismatch of signature on the cheque in question and hence, we are of the firm opinion that the appellate Court was not required to come to the aid and assistance of the appellant for collecting defence evidence at his behest.
The presumptions under the NI Act albeit rebuttable operate in favour of the complainant.
Hence, it is for the accused to rebut such presumptions by leading appropriate defence evidence and the Court cannot be expected to assist the accused to collect evidence on his behalf."

16. Thus, it is clear that Section 391 of Cr.P.C. cannot be pressed to come to rescue of the accused to fill up the lacuna in his defence and to come to aid and assistance for collecting defence evidence for the accused once the accused had opportunity to do the needful during the course of trial.

17. Furthermore, as already noted above in the instant case, the petitioners failed to invoke the provisions of 243 and 247 of Cr.P.C. during the period of 8 years when the trial was pending and also did not file application under Section 391 of Cr.P.C. before the appellate Court for a period of 5 years and filed this application only when the appeal was posted for final arguments.
In the present case on the contrary, the petitioners have duly relied on the bill Ex. D-1 and taken their defence on the basis of the said bill.
They chose to prove the said bill by witness DW/1.
Now at the appellate stage the petitioners want to prove the said bill in a different manner.

This cannot be said to be a bona fide case in terms of Section 391 of Cr.P.C.
18.
So far as the bill Ex. D/1 is concerned, the said bill is already on record and has been exhibited by DW/1.
The petitioners can take all their defence at the time of arguments in the appeal on the basis of the said bill.
It would be for the appellate court while deciding the appeal to examine such issue based on the evidence available on record.
19. As a consequence of the aforesaid, I find no infirmity in the impugned order warranting interference, the revision lacks merit and stands dismissed.

(VIVEK JAIN) JUDGE MISHRA ARVIND KUMAR MISHRA 2024.04.06 11:30:44 +05'30'
